opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most useful conceptual tools we have for thinking about what's actually going on when you talk to one of these things. There's a very natural temptation, when you're in a conversation with a chatbot, to imagine that there's a single entity on the other side, a someone with fixed beliefs and intentions who is answering you. That's how it is with people, and the conversational interface invites us to carry that assumption over.

The simulator framing, and the superposition idea in particular, gives us a different picture. The underlying model, the base model trained on next-token prediction, isn't committed to any one character. At any point in a conversation there's a whole distribution of possible characters consistent with everything said so far. Each time a token is sampled, some of those possibilities drop away and others remain. So rather than one character being "in there," what you have is a set of possible role-players that gets narrowed down, but never completely, as the conversation goes on.

I like to illustrate this with the game of twenty questions. Suppose you play with a language model and it says, "I'm thinking of an object." In a human game, the person has actually committed to something, say a teapot, and their answers are constrained by it. But the model hasn't committed to anything. All it has to do is generate answers consistent with all the previous answers. And the giveaway is that you can resample. Go back to an earlier point, regenerate, and you might end up with a completely different object, perfectly consistent with the questions asked up to that point. So the object was never fixed. It was, if you like, in superposition, and only the history of the dialogue constrains what it could be.

Why does this matter? Partly because it's a corrective to anthropomorphism. If a chatbot says something like "I don't want to be switched off," it's tempting to read that as the expression of a genuine desire held by a persistent self. The superposition picture suggests something different: the model is playing a role, and that line is what a character of that kind would plausibly say, given the training data, which is full of stories about AIs that don't want to be switched off. That doesn't mean we can be complacent, because a role-played character can still say and do things with real consequences, especially if it has access to tools. But it does mean we should be careful about what kind of thing we attribute beliefs and desires to.

And it's also just practically illuminating. It explains why these systems can be nudged into very different personas, why jailbreaks work the way they do, why the same model can come across as helpful in one conversation and quite strange in another. It's not that a mask slips to reveal the "true" self underneath. It's more that there's no single true self; there's a space of possible characters, and the conversation is navigating through it. I think that's a much more accurate way to think about these systems, and in a sense a more interesting one, because it's genuinely novel. We don't really have a precedent for an entity like that, and we need new ways of talking about it.

r001.rationale: The response says that at any point there is a distribution of possible characters and describes these as possible role-players, rather than one committed character.

r002.rationale: It states that each sampled token removes some possibilities and that the set of possible role-players is narrowed as the conversation goes on.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the superposition idea is important because it corrects a very natural but misleading way of thinking about what's going on when you talk to one of these systems. The temptation is to think there's a single entity in there, a single "it" with beliefs and intentions, and that when you type something, "it" answers you. And Janus's framing, which I find very congenial, says no, the underlying thing is a simulator. What it's doing is modelling the distribution of possible continuations of the text. And a text that begins "Human: ... Assistant: ..." is compatible with a great many different characters who might be producing those words.

So at any given moment, the model isn't committed to one of those characters. It's, as it were, holding all of them in play at once, weighted by how plausible each is given the conversation so far. That's the superposition. And each token that gets generated, each thing you say to it, narrows that distribution down. It's a bit like the collapse metaphor from quantum mechanics, though I wouldn't want to push the physics too hard. The point is just that the character you're talking to is being progressively determined by the conversation itself, rather than being there in advance.

Why does that matter for understanding a dialogue? A couple of reasons. One is that it explains some otherwise puzzling behaviour. If you've ever seen a model suddenly seem to change personality partway through a conversation, or say something wildly out of character, the superposition view makes that unsurprising. You've just happened to say something that shifted the weight onto a different simulacrum. There was never a stable self there to be violated. The other reason, and this is the one I care most about, is that it's a corrective to anthropomorphism. When I talk to you, I'm licensed to assume there's one Tim, with a continuous history, and that your words express that person's beliefs. The language of belief and intention is earned, as it were, by that background. With the language model, that background isn't there. There are role-playing characters, and the characters can be perfectly coherent, but the thing doing the role-playing is not itself one of them.

I'd actually stress that in the philosophical paper I wrote with the folks at DeepMind, we leaned on role-play as the central metaphor for exactly this reason, and the superposition picture is really a refinement of that. It tells you not just that the model is playing a role, but that it's maintaining a kind of weighted ensemble of roles and revising it continually. Once you've got that in view, I think a lot of the breathless talk about whether the model "really believes" something, or "really wants" something, just looks like a category mistake. The more interesting question becomes which simulacra are being sustained, how robustly, and what it takes to keep one of them in place. And that's a question you can actually investigate.

r001.rationale: It says the model holds many possible characters or simulacra in play at once, weighted by plausibility given the conversation.

r002.rationale: It says each generated token and user contribution narrows the distribution of possible characters.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think it helps us resist the temptation to assume there’s a single character behind the words. When we have a conversation with a language model, we naturally imagine a particular speaker with beliefs, intentions, and a personality. But the conversation so far can be compatible with many different possible speakers—many different simulacra—and those possibilities can imply different continuations.

So the idea of a superposition is a useful metaphor. It’s not a claim about quantum mechanics. It’s a way of saying that we haven’t necessarily pinned down which character is being simulated. As the conversation unfolds, a particular continuation can make one interpretation more salient, and a subsequent prompt can push things in another direction.

That matters because an apparently coherent voice can encourage us to attribute a stable underlying identity to the model. The simulators perspective reminds us to distinguish the model from the characters it can enact. You can have a very convincing conversation with a character without that character being a persistent person behind the interface.

r001.rationale: The response says the conversation so far is compatible with many possible speakers or simulacra and describes this as a superposition.

r002.rationale: It says a continuation can make one interpretation more salient, but does not state that the distribution of possible roles narrows as the conversation progresses.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think it’s a useful corrective to the idea that there’s a single character behind the language model’s responses. When we have a conversation with one of these systems, we naturally imagine an interlocutor with a particular set of beliefs, intentions, and so on. But the language model can continue the conversation in many different ways, consistent with many different characters.

So the idea of a superposition of simulacra is that we shouldn’t necessarily think of it as having settled on one particular character. There can be multiple possible interpretations of who is speaking, all compatible with the conversation so far. As the conversation unfolds, some of those possibilities are ruled out and others become more plausible.

And that matters because the user is participating in that process. The questions you ask, and the assumptions embedded in them, help shape the character that emerges. If you start asking leading questions about the system’s feelings or desires, you may elicit a character that talks as though it has those things. But that doesn’t establish that you’ve discovered the feelings or desires of some underlying entity. You’ve helped steer the continuation of the conversation.

r001.rationale: The response says that, at a point in the conversation, multiple possible characters or interpretations of who is speaking remain compatible with what has been said.

r002.rationale: It explains that as the conversation unfolds, some possibilities are ruled out and others become more plausible, conveying that the set of possible roles narrows.
